\chapter{The Parts of the Day}
\label{ch:mr-divasache-bhag}
\hlchaptermodality{66}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the parts of the day and say that something happens in one of them.}

From cold: the four parts of the day in the order they happen, the whole day that holds them, and each one turned into an at-that-time word in front of a verb -- including the masculine one that takes -aa where the four feminine ones take -ii.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[sakāḷ]{\mr{सकाळ} (sakāḷ) — morning}

\label{lesson:MR-C66-sakal}



\begin{quote}
You can ask \textbf{\mr{कधी}} — \emph{when} — and you have exactly one word to answer it with: \textbf{\mr{उद्या}}, tomorrow.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{tumhī kadhī yetā?} and answer it
\end{itemize}

That is a question with one answer. This chapter widens the answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{सकाळ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} — \emph{sakāḷ} — \textbf{morning}
\end{quote}

The last letter is \textbf{\mr{ळ}}, the retroflex \emph{l} you first read in \textbf{\mr{काळजी} \mr{घ्या}}. Marathi keeps it where standard Hindi does not — so if you come to Marathi from Hindi, this letter is new, and it is worth slowing down on rather than reading as an ordinary \textbf{\mr{ल}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that means \textquotedblleft{}at that time\textquotedblright{}}]
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} is the morning as a thing. To put an event \emph{in} it, add \textbf{-\mr{ी}}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the part of the day} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} \emph{sakāḷ} & \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} \emph{sakāḷī} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{सकाळी} \mr{येतो}.} — \emph{mī sakāḷī yeto.} — \textbf{I come in the morning.}
\end{quote}

Notice where \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} sits: early, before the verb, in the same slot \textbf{\mr{उद्या}} and \textbf{\mr{कधी}} take. \textbf{A Marathi time word fronts the verb}, and this one is no exception.

English needs two words for that slot — \emph{in the morning}. Marathi needs one letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sakāḷ} — morning
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sakāḷī} — in the morning
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mī sakāḷī yeto}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} and find the \textbf{\mr{ळ}} you already read in \textbf{\mr{काळजी}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\mr{सकाळ}}? (\textbf{Morning}.) What do you add to put something in it? (\textbf{-\mr{ी}} — \emph{sakāḷī}.) And where in the sentence does that word go? (\textbf{Early, in front of the verb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dupār]{\mr{दुपार} (dupār) — afternoon}

\label{lesson:MR-C66-dupar}



\begin{quote}
Say the morning. Then say \emph{in} the morning, and listen for the letter that does the work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{दुपार}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{दुपार}} — \emph{dupār} — \textbf{afternoon}, the middle of the day
\end{quote}

It is the stretch after the morning and before the evening — the middle of the day, when the sun is highest.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{दुपारी} \mr{येतो}.} — \emph{mī dupārī yeto.} — \textbf{I come in the afternoon.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending holds}]
You were shown \textbf{-\mr{ी}} on one word. Here it is on a second, doing the same job:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the part of the day} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} \emph{sakāḷ} & \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} \emph{sakāḷī} \\
\textbf{\mr{दुपार}} \emph{dupār} & \textbf{\mr{दुपारी}} \emph{dupārī} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two is where a pattern starts being worth trusting. \textbf{Expect the next part of the day to behave the same way}, and you will be right twice more before this chapter is over.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dupār} — afternoon
  \item \emph{dupārī} — in the afternoon
  \item \emph{mī dupārī yeto}
  \item both parts of the day so far, in the order they happen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\mr{दुपार}}? (\textbf{Afternoon}.) How do you say \emph{in the afternoon}? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{दुपारी}}}.) Which ending did you use, and had you seen it before? (\textbf{-\mr{ी}}, and \textbf{yes} — on \emph{sakāḷī}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sandhyākāḷ]{\mr{संध्याकाळ} (sandhyākāḷ) — evening}

\label{lesson:MR-C66-sandhyakal}



\begin{quote}
Two parts of the day, and their at-that-time forms. Say all four words before you turn to the new one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{संध्याकाळ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}} — \emph{sandhyākāḷ} — \textbf{evening}
\end{quote}

It is the longest word in this chapter, and \textbf{you have already read half of it.} Look at its end:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\mr{स}\textbf{\mr{काळ}} & \emph{sa-\textbf{kāḷ}} \\
\mr{संध्या}\textbf{\mr{काळ}} & \emph{sandhyā-\textbf{kāḷ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The morning and the evening \textbf{end in the same piece — \mr{काळ}}. Once you see that, \mr{संध्याकाळ} stops being a long new word and becomes a short new piece — \textbf{\mr{संध्या}} — in front of one you can already read.

That is worth doing to any long word in this language before deciding it is hard: look for the part of it you have met.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: third time, same ending}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{संध्याकाळी} \mr{येतो}.} — \emph{mī sandhyākāḷī yeto.} — \textbf{I come in the evening.}
\end{quote}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the part of the day} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} & \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} \\
\textbf{\mr{दुपार}} & \textbf{\mr{दुपारी}} \\
\textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}} & \textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळी}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three for three. The ending has not cared how long the word was, where the stress fell, or what letter came before it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sandhyākāḷ} — evening
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sandhyākāḷī} — in the evening
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} and \textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}}, and find where they stop differing
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three parts of the day so far, in the order they happen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}}? (\textbf{Evening}.) Which earlier word does it end like? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}}}.) Say \emph{I come in the evening}. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{संध्याकाळी} \mr{येतो}}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rātra]{\mr{रात्र} (rātra) — night}

\label{lesson:MR-C66-ratra}



\begin{quote}
Three parts of the day are yours. Say them in order, and then name the one still missing from the end of it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{रात्र}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{रात्र}} — \emph{rātra} — \textbf{night}
\end{quote}

The word ends on \textbf{\mr{त्र}}, a \textbf{\mr{त}} and a \textbf{\mr{र}} written as one joined shape. You have read that join before; here it closes the word rather than opening it, so give it its full value — \emph{rā-tra}, not \emph{rāt}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{रात्री} \mr{येतो}.} — \emph{mī rātrī yeto.} — \textbf{I come at night.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four for four, and what English does instead}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the part of the day} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} & \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} \\
\textbf{\mr{दुपार}} & \textbf{\mr{दुपारी}} \\
\textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}} & \textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळी}} \\
\textbf{\mr{रात्र}} & \textbf{\mr{रात्री}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four words, one ending, no exceptions among them.

Now look at what English needed for that same column: \emph{in} the morning, \emph{in} the afternoon, \emph{in} the evening — but \textbf{at} night. English changes its preposition and Marathi does not change anything. \textbf{The irregular language here is the one you already speak.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rātra} — night
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{rātrī} — at night
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four parts of the day, in order
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four at-that-time forms, in the same order
  \item \emph{Notice:} which language needed a different word for the last one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{I come at night}. (\emph{\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{रात्री} \mr{येतो}}}.) How many of the four parts of the day take \textbf{-\mr{ी}}? (\textbf{All four}.) Which language had to change a word to say the same set? (\textbf{English} — \emph{in} the morning, but \emph{at} night.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[divas]{\mr{दिवस} (divas) — day}

\label{lesson:MR-C66-divas}



\begin{quote}
Four parts, four at-that-time words. Say them. Then ask yourself what the four of them together are called.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{दिवस}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{दिवस}} — \emph{divas} — \textbf{day}
\end{quote}

Not a fifth part. \textbf{The whole that holds the other four} — the morning, the afternoon, the evening and the night are stretches of a \mr{दिवस}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one that will not take -\mr{ी}}]
Four words took \textbf{-\mr{ी}} without complaint. This one does not:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{रात्र}} & \textbf{\mr{रात्री}} \\
\textbf{\mr{दिवस}} & \textbf{\mr{दिवसा}} — \emph{divasā}, by day \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-\mr{आ}}, not \textbf{-\mr{ी}}. And the reason is one you already own.

\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}, \mr{दुपार}, \mr{संध्याकाळ}} and \textbf{\mr{रात्र}} are all \textbf{feminine}. \textbf{\mr{दिवस}} is \textbf{masculine} — and gender is the thing that has decided endings for you since the chapter that gave you three of them.

So this is not the pattern breaking. It is the pattern meeting a noun of a different gender and doing what it has always done. \textbf{An exception you can predict is not an exception.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{divas} — day
  \item \emph{divasā} — by day
  \item the four parts a \emph{divas} is made of
  \item which gender each of the five words is
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\mr{दिवस}} a part of the day? (\textbf{No} — it is the whole of it.) Why does it take \textbf{-\mr{आ}} and not \textbf{-\mr{ी}}? (\textbf{It is masculine}; the four parts are feminine.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[divasāce bhāg]{(the parts of the day) — from cold}

\label{lesson:MR-R66-day-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Name the parts of the day you have, in the order they happen.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending, every part of the day}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the part of the day} & \textbf{at that time} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\mr{सकाळ}} \emph{sakāḷ} & \textbf{\mr{सकाळी}} \emph{sakāḷī} \\
\textbf{\mr{दुपार}} \emph{dupār} & \textbf{\mr{दुपारी}} \emph{dupārī} \\
\textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळ}} \emph{sandhyākāḷ} & \textbf{\mr{संध्याकाळी}} \emph{sandhyākāḷī} \\
\textbf{\mr{रात्र}} \emph{rātra} & \textbf{\mr{रात्री}} \emph{rātrī} \\
\textbf{\mr{दिवस}} \emph{divas} & \textbf{\mr{दिवसा}} \emph{divasā} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The left column names a stretch of the day. The right column \textbf{puts something inside it}, and for the four feminine parts the only difference is \textbf{-\mr{ी}}.

The last row is the whole day rather than a part of it, it is masculine, and it takes \textbf{-\mr{आ}}. Gender picked that, the way it has picked endings for you all along.

Then that word goes early, in front of the verb — the slot \textbf{\mr{कधी}} and \textbf{\mr{उद्या}} have taken since your first chapter. So a sentence about when something happens has the same shape every time, and only one word in it is new.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four parts of the day, in order, then the word for the whole
  \item each one again as an at-that-time word, and hear which one differs
  \item \emph{mī sakāḷī yeto}, then the same with the afternoon
  \item where the time word sits, without looking
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending puts an event inside a part of the day? (\textbf{-\mr{ी}}.) Which of the five words refuses it, and why? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{दिवस}}} — \textbf{masculine}.) And does the time word go before or after the verb? (\textbf{Before}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
